_README: Characterisation technique library — Roadmap P9. Every record must state what the technique CANNOT tell you; the health check refuses a record without it. That field is the reason this library exists: almost every characterisation mistake in this field is a technique applied outside what it can answer, and the answer still looks like a result. DRAFT — pending review by the research group.
_note_on_numbers: This library deliberately contains almost no numeric specifications. Resolution, detection limit and spot size are properties of a particular instrument and configuration, not of a technique, and quoting them here would invite someone to cite a number that does not describe the machine they used. Where a number is definitional it is given as such. Fill in your own instruments' figures from their manuals.

items.name: Powder X-ray diffraction
items.summary: Identifies crystalline phases and measures lattice parameters from the angles at which X-rays diffract off periodic planes.
items.probes: monochromatic X-rays over a range of incident angles
answers: Which crystalline phases are present, by matching peak positions and relative intensities against reference patterns
Lattice parameters, and how they change with composition or state of charge
Whether a material is crystalline at all
An estimate of crystallite size from peak broadening, once instrumental broadening is subtracted
cannotTell: How much AMORPHOUS material is present. Amorphous content produces a broad hump, not peaks, and can dominate a sample whose pattern looks clean. A phase-pure-looking pattern is not evidence of a phase-pure sample.

Particle size. Scherrer broadening gives a CRYSTALLITE size — the coherently diffracting domain. One particle can contain many crystallites, so the two numbers routinely differ by an order of magnitude and are not interchangeable.
The surface. XRD averages over the illuminated volume; a surface layer thin enough to govern the electrochemistry is usually invisible in it.
Whether a shift comes from strain or from composition. Both move peaks. One pattern cannot separate them — that needs a series, or a complementary measurement.
Phase identity on its own for a new material. Matching a database pattern is evidence, not proof, especially where several phases have similar patterns.
Anything about elements too light to scatter strongly. Lithium is nearly invisible to X-rays, so lithium positions in a structure are inferred, not seen.

sample.form: Dry powder, or a coated electrode measured directly
sample.amount: Enough to fill the holder to a flat, level surface
sample.prep: Grind gently to a fine, uniform powder and pack flat. Poor packing and preferred orientation change RELATIVE intensities without moving the peaks — which is why an intensity mismatch against a reference pattern is common and usually not a phase problem.
sample.destructive: Non-destructive to the material, though grinding changes it
sample.notes: An air-sensitive material needs an air-tight holder or a dome. Measuring it in air and then explaining the extra peaks afterwards is not a workaround.

reportWith: Radiation source and wavelength
The 2θ range and step size
Whether the pattern is background-subtracted, and how
For any Scherrer estimate: the peak used, the shape factor assumed, and the instrumental broadening correction
Reference pattern identifiers for every phase assigned
misread: Reporting Scherrer crystallite size as particle size
Calling a sample phase-pure when only crystalline phases were measured
Fitting an amorphous hump as background and then not mentioning it
Assigning a phase on peak positions alone when relative intensities do not match

materialNotes.material.nafepo4: The record states that only the olivine polymorph cycles and maricite does not — same formula, different structure. XRD is what tells the two apart, and "NaFePO₄" alone does not identify the material.
materialNotes.material.silicon: The record notes the crystalline starting material does not come back after the first cycle. Post-cycling XRD is how that is established rather than assumed.
materialNotes.material.nnfm: The record notes several phase transitions across the sodium content range; which phases are present is an XRD question.
materialNotes.material.graphite_k: This record quotes its capacity per the stage-1 compound KC₈, and notes the larger ion expands the lattice far more than lithium does. Staging and lattice expansion are both read from peak positions.
materialNotes.material.mno2: This record states it cannot distinguish the α, β, γ, δ and λ polymorphs — same formula, different behaviour. Distinguishing them is the XRD question.
materialNotes.material.ni_oh2: This record names the α and β hydroxide phases and the γ oxyhydroxide as having different capacities and different swelling. Which phase you have is an XRD answer.
materialNotes.material.nvp: This record attributes the rate capability and cycle life to a framework that changes volume very little. That is a lattice-parameter claim, and only in-situ or post-cycling XRD tests it.
materialNotes.material.pb: This record names sulfation — coarse lead sulfate that will not reduce — as the dominant failure. XRD identifies the PbSO₄ phase; SEM shows how coarse it has become.

items.name: Scanning electron microscopy
items.summary: Images surface topography by scanning a focused electron beam and collecting the electrons that come back.
items.probes: a focused electron beam raster-scanned across the surface
items.detects: secondary electrons (topography) or backscattered electrons (composition contrast)
answers: Surface morphology: particle shape, agglomeration, coating uniformity, cracking
Whether an electrode coating is continuous, and how the binder is distributed
Relative atomic-number contrast, in backscattered mode
Cross-sectional structure, if the sample is sectioned or fractured
cannotTell: What anything is made of. Composition contrast in backscattered mode is relative, not identification — that requires EDS, with its own limits.
Crystal structure. A well-faceted particle is not evidence of a phase.
The interior. An SEM image is of a surface; unless the sample is sectioned, what is underneath is unknown.
Anything three-dimensional with confidence. An image is a projection, and apparent thickness, depth and overlap are all ambiguous in one.

Whether what you photographed is representative. Choosing the field of view is an act of selection, and a single image of a good region is a claim about the whole sample that the image does not support.
The electrochemically relevant surface. What the electrolyte reaches is not what the detector sees.

sample.amount: A small quantity on a stub, or a mounted electrode disc
sample.prep: Non-conducting samples charge under the beam and need a conductive coating — which then hides fine surface detail and adds features of its own, so what the coating is must be reported.
sample.destructive: Usually non-destructive, but beam damage and contamination are real for soft materials
sample.notes: Powder must be firmly attached. Loose powder in the chamber is both a bad image and a service call.

reportWith: Accelerating voltage and detector mode
Working distance and magnification — always with a scale bar, never magnification alone
Any conductive coating and its material
How many fields of view were examined before the one shown was chosen
misread: Publishing one image as characteristic of a batch
Reading particle size off an image without a counted, stated distribution
Attributing a feature to the material when it was introduced by the coating or the beam
Quoting magnification instead of a scale bar — magnification depends on the display size and means nothing on its own

materialNotes.material.silicon: The record puts particle fracture from a threefold volume change at the centre of the failure mode. SEM is where cracking is seen.
materialNotes.material.zn_metal: The record names dendrites and passivation as the limits on aqueous zinc.
materialNotes.material.li_metal: Dendrite and dead-metal morphology after cycling.
materialNotes.material.pb: The record describes sulfation as the GROWTH OF COARSE crystals. Coarseness is a morphology observation, not a phase one.
materialNotes.material.pbo2: This record names softening and shedding of the positive active mass as the usual end of life — a structural change in the electrode, visible where a capacity number is not.
materialNotes.material.sulfur: This record notes the volume change on conversion to Li₂S is large. What that does to the electrode is a morphology question.

items.name: Transmission electron microscopy
items.summary: Images the internal structure of very thin specimens with electrons transmitted through them, and can diffract from the same region to identify what it is.
items.probes: a high-energy electron beam transmitted through an electron-transparent specimen
items.detects: transmitted and diffracted electrons — bright-field images, lattice fringes, and diffraction patterns from a selected area
answers: Internal structure at a scale SEM cannot reach: core–shell arrangements, coating thickness, internal porosity
Lattice fringes, and from their spacing a d-spacing that can be compared with a known structure
Phase identification from a selected-area diffraction pattern of the region imaged
Whether nanoparticles are single-crystalline, polycrystalline or amorphous
cannotTell: Anything about the bulk. A TEM grid holds nanograms, and the regions thin enough to image are a biased subset of those. Extrapolating a TEM observation to a batch is the most common overreach with this technique.
What the material was before the beam hit it. Beam damage, heating and reduction under the beam are routine, particularly for oxides and organics, so the specimen can change while it is being imaged.
Phase identity from lattice fringes alone. A fringe spacing is one number; several phases can share it. Indexing needs a diffraction pattern or an FFT with more than one reflection.
Bulk composition. EDS in the TEM measures the thin region illuminated, which was selected for being thin.
Three-dimensional structure from a single image, since everything through the thickness is superimposed in projection.

sample.form: Electron-transparent — nanoparticles dispersed on a grid, or a thinned lamella
sample.amount: Vanishingly small; this is the crux of the sampling problem
sample.prep: Dispersion quality governs what you see. Agglomerates that survive dispersion are indistinguishable from agglomerates that were in the material.
sample.destructive: The specimen is consumed by preparation, and often altered by the beam
sample.notes: Air-sensitive materials need a transfer holder; a specimen that oxidised on the way in is a different specimen.

reportWith: Accelerating voltage
How the specimen was dispersed or thinned
For any d-spacing: how it was measured, and which reflections were indexed
How many particles were examined, and how they were selected
misread: Presenting one particle as the material
Identifying a phase from a single lattice spacing
Not reporting beam-sensitivity when the material is known to be beam-sensitive
Measuring a coating thickness at one point and quoting it without a distribution

items.name: Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy
items.summary: Identifies which elements are present, and roughly in what proportion, from the characteristic X-rays an electron beam excites. Almost always an attachment to an SEM or TEM.
items.probes: the same electron beam as the microscope it is attached to
items.detects: characteristic X-ray energies, and their counts
answers: Which elements above the detector's cutoff are present
An approximate ratio between heavier elements
Where those elements are, as a map — the most useful mode for checking whether a coating is where you think it is
cannotTell: Anything about hydrogen, helium or lithium. They are not detectable by conventional EDS. For lithium-ion work this is a hard limit: the element the experiment is about is invisible.

Reliable quantities for light elements generally. Oxygen, carbon and nitrogen quantification is poor, and carbon is further confounded by the conductive coating and by hydrocarbon contamination in the chamber.

Composition at a point. The interaction volume that generates X-rays is far larger than the beam spot, so a 'point' analysis includes a pear-shaped region of everything around and beneath it — on a rough or particulate sample, that includes the substrate.
Oxidation state, bonding, or which compound the elements are in. That needs XPS, XRD or spectroscopy.
Whether a light-element map means anything at all. Carbon and oxygen maps in particular are more often contamination and topography than composition.

sample.form: Same as the microscope it is in
sample.amount: Same as the microscope it is in
sample.prep: A flat, polished surface is required for anything approaching quantitative analysis. On loose powder the result is qualitative.
sample.destructive: No, beyond the microscope's own beam effects
sample.notes: Standardless quantification is a calculation with assumptions, not a measurement. Treat the numbers as semi-quantitative unless standards were run.

reportWith: That it is EDS and whether the quantification was standardless
Accelerating voltage — it sets the interaction volume and which lines are excited
Whether the surface was flat and polished
The conductive coating material, so its element is not read as sample composition
misread: Quoting atomic percentages to two decimal places from a standardless analysis on rough powder
Concluding a material is lithium-free because EDS did not see lithium
Reading a carbon map on a carbon-coated sample as the material's carbon
Using a point spectrum on a particle smaller than the interaction volume

items.name: Nitrogen physisorption — BET surface area and pore analysis
items.summary: Measures how much gas a surface adsorbs at a series of pressures, and converts that isotherm into a specific surface area and a pore-size distribution.
items.probes: nitrogen gas at successive relative pressures, at its boiling point of 77 K
items.detects: the quantity of gas adsorbed and desorbed — the isotherm
answers: A specific surface area, on the assumptions of the BET model
The shape of the isotherm, which is itself the most informative output and should always be shown
A pore-size distribution, once a model is chosen and stated
Total pore volume, and the split between micropores and larger pores
cannotTell: The ELECTROCHEMICALLY ACCESSIBLE area. This is the one that matters here. Nitrogen at 77 K reaches pores a solvated ion at room temperature cannot enter, and wetting can exclude regions nitrogen entered freely. A high BET area is not a promise of high capacitance, and the correlation between them across materials is weak.

A defensible surface area for a strongly microporous material. The BET model assumes multilayer physisorption on an open surface; in micropores the pores fill instead, so the model's assumptions do not hold. The number is still universally reported — which is a convention, not a justification — and the pressure range used has to be stated because it changes the answer.
A pore size independent of the model. BJH, DFT and NLDFT applied to the same isotherm give different distributions. The model is part of the result and must be reported with it.
Anything about pores that nitrogen cannot enter within the measurement, including closed porosity.
Whether the sample was properly degassed. Incomplete degassing lowers the measured area, and it leaves no signature in the final number.

sample.amount: Enough total surface area for a good measurement — a low-area material needs a lot more mass than a high-area one
sample.prep: Degassing under vacuum or flowing gas, at a temperature and for a time that must both be reported. Too gentle leaves adsorbed water and understates the area; too harsh changes the material.
sample.destructive: Non-destructive if degassing conditions were mild enough — which is a judgement, not a given
sample.notes: Measuring a whole electrode rather than the active powder measures the binder and the conductive additive too.

reportWith: Adsorptive gas and temperature
Degassing temperature, duration and atmosphere
The relative-pressure range used for the BET fit
The model used for any pore-size distribution
The isotherm itself — a surface area quoted without its isotherm cannot be checked
misread: Presenting BET area as if it were the electrochemically active area
Comparing BET areas measured after different degassing conditions
Quoting a pore size without naming the model that produced it
Explaining a capacitance difference by a BET-area difference alone

materialNotes.material.hard_carbon: The record attributes part of the capacity to filling of CLOSED pores — which is precisely the porosity BET cannot see, since nitrogen cannot enter them. A useful case of a technique whose limitation is the point.

items.name: Raman spectroscopy
items.summary: Probes vibrational modes through inelastic scattering of laser light — the standard tool for carbon materials and for distinguishing polymorphs.
items.probes: a monochromatic laser focused to a small spot
items.detects: inelastically scattered light, as a shift in wavenumber
answers: Which vibrational modes are present, and so which bonding environments
For carbons, the D and G bands and their intensity ratio — a widely used descriptor of disorder
Polymorph discrimination where phases differ in symmetry but are hard to separate by XRD
Local information, since the probe is a focused spot rather than a bulk average
cannotTell: A quantitative phase fraction, without a calibration built for that specific mixture and instrument.

A transferable I_D/I_G. The ratio depends on the excitation wavelength, the fitting procedure and whether peak height or integrated area was used. It is comparable within one study on one instrument; between studies it usually is not.
Anything, if the sample fluoresces. Fluorescence can bury the Raman signal entirely, and a flat, featureless spectrum is a measurement failure rather than a finding.
What the material was before the laser hit it. Focused laser power heats, oxidises and transforms — carbons and oxides especially — so a power series is a control, not an optional extra.
Bulk composition. The spot samples a very small volume; several spots are needed before any statement about the sample.

sample.form: Powder, film or electrode, measured directly
sample.amount: Very little — a single particle suffices
sample.prep: Usually none, which is much of its appeal
sample.destructive: Non-destructive at low power; destructive at high power, sometimes without an obvious sign
sample.notes: Always run a laser-power series and show that the spectrum does not change with power.

reportWith: Excitation wavelength and laser power at the sample
Acquisition time and number of accumulations
How many spots were measured
For any band ratio: how the bands were fitted, and whether heights or areas were used
misread: Comparing I_D/I_G values between papers using different lasers
Reporting a spectrum from one spot as the sample's spectrum
Attributing a change to the material when it was caused by laser heating
Treating band intensity as concentration without calibration

materialNotes.material.hard_carbon: The record states that behaviour varies strongly with precursor and pyrolysis temperature. The D and G band ratio is the standard probe of that disorder — though it is a fingerprint, not a measure of capacity.
materialNotes.material.graphite: Distinguishes graphitic ordering from disorder, which is what separates graphite from the hard carbons above it.

items.name: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
items.summary: Measures the binding energies of electrons ejected from the outermost few nanometres, giving elemental composition and chemical state of the surface.
items.detects: the kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons, converted to binding energy
answers: Which elements are present at the surface, and in what proportion
Chemical state and local bonding, from binding-energy shifts
Surface composition depth-profiles, if combined with ion sputtering
The composition of interfacial layers such as an SEI — the main reason this technique appears in battery work
cannotTell: Anything about the bulk. The information depth is a few nanometres. A bulk claim from XPS is a category error, however good the spectrum.

A binding energy independent of your referencing choice. Insulating samples charge, and the correction — commonly to adventitious carbon — is a convention with real disagreement about it. Two labs can report different states for the same surface from the same raw data.

A unique peak fit. Component fitting is under-determined: several sets of components fit the same envelope acceptably. Constraints have to be declared, and a good residual is not evidence the assignment is right.

The surface you care about, if it was exposed to air. Air-sensitive surfaces change on transfer, so a sample not moved under inert conditions gives you the composition of a surface that formed on the way to the instrument.
What sputtering did to the sample. Ion sputtering for depth profiling preferentially removes some species and can reduce others, so a depth profile is a profile of the sputtered sample.

sample.amount: A small piece or a pressed powder
sample.prep: Air-sensitive samples must be transferred without air exposure. Everything else is about avoiding contamination — handling, adhesive and solvent residues all end up in the spectrum.
sample.destructive: Non-destructive without sputtering; destructive with it
sample.notes: Cycled electrodes should be rinsed by a stated procedure — the rinse removes electrolyte salt that would otherwise dominate, and also removes some of what you wanted to measure.

reportWith: X-ray source and pass energy
The charge-referencing method and the value used
For every fit: the component constraints, the background type, and the residual
Transfer conditions for air-sensitive samples
Rinsing procedure for cycled electrodes
misread: Making bulk composition claims from a surface technique
Assigning a chemical state from a peak position without stating the referencing
Fitting many components until the residual is small and presenting that as identification
Comparing surface compositions of samples transferred under different conditions

materialNotes.material.li_metal: The record makes the interphase the whole story. XPS is the standard surface probe of what that layer is made of — on a sample that must never meet air between the glovebox and the instrument.
materialNotes.material.na_metal: The record notes sodium’s interphase is more soluble in common electrolytes than lithium’s.
materialNotes.material.lto: This record attributes LTO’s cycle life to forming little or no interphase, because it operates above the potential where carbonates reduce. "Little or no interphase" is a surface claim, and XPS is how it is tested rather than assumed.
materialNotes.material.nmc111: This record notes nickel-rich layered oxides form surface carbonate and hydroxide in storage, consuming lithium before the experiment starts.

items.name: Thermogravimetric analysis
items.summary: Records mass against temperature in a controlled atmosphere — used for composition splits, thermal stability, and carbon or water content.
items.probes: a programmed temperature ramp in a chosen atmosphere
answers: How much mass is lost, and over which temperature ranges
Carbon content, when combustion in air is complete and the residue is stable
Water and solvent content, from low-temperature loss
Thermal stability limits, in the atmosphere tested
cannotTell: WHAT was lost. TGA weighs; it does not identify. Attributing a mass loss to a species is an inference unless the evolved gas was analysed by a coupled MS or FTIR.
A result independent of the atmosphere and heating rate. Both change onset temperatures and can change the residue. Two TGA curves are comparable only if both were run the same way.
Two overlapping processes apart. Where temperature ranges overlap, a single curve gives a combined loss, and a derivative curve suggests but does not prove a separation.
A trustworthy small mass change without a blank. Buoyancy changes as gas density falls with temperature, producing apparent mass changes of the same order as small real ones.
Anything about a sample that reacted with its crucible, which happens more often than it is reported.

sample.amount: A few milligrams — small enough for uniform heating, large enough for a good signal
sample.prep: Minimal, but the packing and the crucible material both matter
sample.notes: Run a blank with an empty crucible under identical conditions and subtract it.

reportWith: Atmosphere and flow rate
Heating rate and temperature range
Sample mass and crucible material
Whether a blank was subtracted
Any coupled evolved-gas analysis
misread: Naming what was lost without evolved-gas analysis
Comparing onset temperatures from different heating rates
Reading a small mass change that is within the buoyancy artefact
Reporting a composition split from overlapping loss steps as if the split were resolved

materialNotes.material.pba_nafe: The record states that real frameworks contain vacancies and coordinated water, so the formula unit in the denominator of the theoretical capacity is usually not the one in the beaker. TGA is how the water content is measured.
materialNotes.material.lifepo4: This record notes that carbon coating and particle-size reduction exist to solve an electronic-conductivity problem, and that those additions reduce the capacity per gram of ELECTRODE while leaving the theoretical figure unchanged. How much carbon is present is a TGA measurement.
materialNotes.material.ntp: This record states carbon coating changes the rate behaviour dramatically and that coated and uncoated samples are not comparable — so the coating fraction has to be measured, not assumed.
materialNotes.material.sulfur: This record demands the sulfur areal loading be reported before a number can be interpreted. In a sulfur–carbon composite that starts with knowing the sulfur fraction.

items.name: Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy
items.summary: Identifies functional groups from infrared absorption by molecular vibrations.
items.probes: infrared light across a range of wavenumbers
answers: Which functional groups are present
Whether a binder, a surface functionalisation or a residual solvent is there
Qualitative changes to bonding after treatment or cycling
Identification by comparison against a reference spectrum of a known compound
cannotTell: The compound. FTIR identifies functional groups; several compounds share a set. Identification requires a reference spectrum of the actual candidate, and preferably a second technique.
A concentration, without a calibration series. Band intensity depends on path length, contact and scattering as much as on how much is there.

Anything below the surface, in ATR mode. ATR samples only the layer in optical contact with the crystal, and the depth is wavelength-dependent, so a poorly contacted sample gives a weak spectrum of the parts that touched.
A band position that means the same in every environment. Hydrogen bonding, crystallinity and neighbouring groups all shift bands, so a shift is not automatically a chemical change.
A useful spectrum through strong water absorption, which overlaps regions of interest and is very hard to remove convincingly.

sample.form: Powder, film, liquid, or a pressed pellet
sample.prep: Transmission usually needs a KBr pellet; ATR needs firm contact and little else. The mode should be reported, because the two do not give identical spectra.
sample.destructive: Non-destructive in ATR; the pellet is consumed in transmission
sample.notes: Dry the sample and the KBr — adsorbed water shows up strongly and is easily read as sample chemistry.

reportWith: Mode (ATR or transmission) and, for ATR, the crystal material
Resolution and number of scans
Background conditions
Any baseline correction or ATR correction applied
misread: Identifying a compound from functional groups alone
Comparing ATR and transmission spectra as if they were equivalent
Reading adsorbed water as a sample feature
Quantifying from band height without a calibration

items.name: Particle-size analysis
items.summary: Measures a distribution of particle sizes in suspension, by laser diffraction for larger particles or dynamic light scattering for finer ones.
items.probes: laser light through a dispersed suspension
items.detects: the scattering pattern (diffraction) or the fluctuation rate of scattered intensity (DLS)
answers: A size distribution, and percentile descriptors such as D10, D50 and D90
Whether a powder is broadly or narrowly distributed
Whether a dispersion procedure changed the apparent size — which is itself informative about agglomeration
cannotTell: A size that means anything for a non-spherical particle. Both techniques report an equivalent-sphere diameter — the diameter of a sphere that would scatter the same way. For plates, rods or flakes that number corresponds to no dimension anyone could measure with a ruler.
Whether you measured primary particles or agglomerates. The answer depends entirely on the dispersion: sonication time and dispersant change the distribution, so the procedure IS part of the result.

A number comparable with another technique. Laser diffraction, DLS and image analysis routinely give different D50 values for the same powder, because each is defined differently. The technique must be reported with the number.
A reliable distribution for a broad or multimodal powder by DLS, which is strongly biased towards larger scatterers and can miss a fine population entirely.
Anything about shape, which for electrode processing often matters more than size.

sample.form: Powder dispersed in a compatible liquid
sample.amount: Small, but enough to reach the instrument's obscuration window
sample.prep: Dispersion is the measurement. Sonication power and time, the dispersant, and the settling time all change the answer and all have to be recorded.
sample.destructive: Non-destructive to the material, though sonication can break friable agglomerates
sample.notes: For laser diffraction the optical model needs the material's refractive index; an assumed value propagates into the distribution.

reportWith: Technique, and for laser diffraction the optical model and refractive indices used
Dispersant, sonication conditions and settling time
Whether the distribution is by volume or by number — they look completely different for the same powder
D10, D50 and D90 together, never D50 alone
misread: Quoting D50 alone as 'the particle size'
Comparing a DLS number with an SEM-counted number
Reporting a volume distribution and a number distribution interchangeably
Not reporting sonication, then being unable to reproduce the result

materialNotes.material.lifepo4: This record names particle-size reduction as one of the two things done to work around the conductivity limit — so the distribution is a variable of the sample, not a fixed property of the material.

items.name: Inductively coupled plasma spectroscopy
items.summary: Quantifies elemental content in a digested sample, by emission or by mass spectrometry — the reference method when composition must actually be quantitative.
items.probes: a high-temperature plasma that atomises and excites a nebulised solution
items.detects: emitted light at element-characteristic wavelengths, or ions by mass
answers: Quantitative elemental concentrations, including light elements EDS cannot see — lithium among them
Trace-level impurities, at levels no microscope-based technique reaches
Transition-metal dissolution into an electrolyte, a standard degradation measurement
Stoichiometry of a synthesised compound, against calibration standards
cannotTell: Where the element was. The sample is dissolved: all spatial information is gone.
What compound the element was in. ICP gives total elemental content, not speciation or oxidation state.
Anything correct, if digestion was incomplete. Undigested residue silently under-reports whatever was in it, and the result still looks like a clean number with a small uncertainty.
A concentration outside the calibrated range, where the response is not linear.
An accurate result where the matrix interferes — high salt loads and isobaric overlaps in ICP-MS both need a stated strategy, not a hope.

sample.form: A solution — the sample must be digested first
sample.amount: Milligrams, weighed accurately, since the result is normalised to that mass
sample.prep: Acid digestion, usually with heat or microwave assistance. This is the step that determines whether the answer is right.
sample.notes: Run digestion blanks and a certified reference material where one exists for the matrix.

reportWith: Digestion procedure — acids, temperature, duration, vessel
Whether any residue remained after digestion
Calibration standards and range
Blank levels and, where used, the certified reference material recovery
The sample mass used for normalisation
misread: Reporting a stoichiometry from an incomplete digestion
Quoting more significant figures than the mass weighing supports
Treating total metal content as active-material content
Omitting blanks when reporting trace levels

materialNotes.material.lco: The record names cobalt dissolution into the electrolyte as an irreversible loss that does not show in early cycles. ICP on the recovered electrolyte is how dissolution is quantified.
materialNotes.material.lmo: The record names manganese dissolution, worse with temperature and pH.
materialNotes.material.v2o5: The record notes vanadium leaving the electrode into aqueous electrolyte — visible as colour, quantified by ICP.
materialNotes.material.ltp: This record warns that titanium phosphates dissolve slowly in acid and that a short experiment will not reveal it. ICP on the recovered electrolyte is how a slow loss is caught.
materialNotes.material.mno2: This record notes that where manganese dissolves and redeposits, "capacity per gram of MnO₂" quotes a mass that does not stay constant. ICP is how you find out whether it did.
materialNotes.material.nmc111: This record names transition metals dissolving from the cathode and poisoning the anode interphase — so the cathode fault appears as anode degradation.
materialNotes.material.ni_oh2: This record notes the practical electrode contains cobalt additives, so the composition of the active mass is not the formula on the label.
materialNotes.material.lifepo4: This record names iron dissolution as something an aqueous cell suffers that a non-aqueous one never sees.

closing: No technique here answers a question on its own. Each measures one thing about one part of a sample under one set of conditions, and the sentence you write in a paper is usually a claim about the material as a whole. Bridging that gap is what the 'cannot tell you' list on each page is for — read it before choosing the technique, not after the reviewer asks.
_materialNotes: Why THIS technique is relevant to THAT material — and the rule that keeps it honest: a link exists only where the material's own record names the thing the technique measures. Nothing here says what a measurement showed. These are reasons to run an experiment, never results of one.
